title: Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items in children and adults
research_question: To investigate the roles of attention capture, serial order retention, and phonological processing in the Irrelevant Speech Effect (ISE) by testing the effects of task-irrelevant steady-state and changing-state speech on serial order reconstruction of verbal and spatial items in children and adults.

participants.description: 83 adults (50 females, aged 19-32 years) and 81 third-grade children (44 females, mean age 8 years, 10 months, SD 9 months). All native German speakers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing. Verbal task: 43 adults, 30 children. Spatial task: 40 adults, 51 children.
participants.recruitment: Adults: students and staff of the University of Kaiserslautern. Children: three primary schools in the Kaiserslautern region.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Consonant-vowel (CV) syllables (/ba:/, /be:/, /bi:/, etc.) produced by a trained female speaker. Changing-state trials: random sequence of different syllables. Steady-state trials: repetition of single syllable (/ba:/). 200-ms silent interval between syllables. Average sound level 62 dB LAeq. Silence condition also used.

Colored drawings representing 16 monosyllabic German words (e.g., Bett, Bus, Eis, Frosch, Kamm, Mond, Pilz, Schal, Schiff, Zaun, Brief, Haus, Herz, Hut, Nuss, Schwein) for the verbal task. Presented pictorially to avoid reading ability impacts.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Methods - Serial order reconstruction tasks, p. 5

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Black dots (10-mm diameter) on a white background within a 304 × 183 mm black frame, drawn from 80 possible locations on an 8 × 10 grid, for the spatial task.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Methods - Serial order reconstruction tasks, p. 5

measures.instrument: Proportion of items recalled at the correct serial position in a serial order reconstruction task (verbal or spatial).

mechanisms: Irrelevant speech interferes with mechanisms or memory traces specific to the verbal domain, such as articulatory rehearsal and/or the integrity of phonological representations.
Children are more susceptible to interference from irrelevant speech than adults due to less specified phonological representations, making them more vulnerable to disruption.
High performers rely more on phonological strategies, making them more prone to disruption by irrelevant speech.
moderators: Sound condition (silence, steady-state speech, changing-state speech)
Individual short-term memory capacity (estimated by serial recall performance in quiet)
implementation_implications: The findings suggest that irrelevant speech specifically impairs verbal working memory, which has implications for learning environments where verbal information processing is critical.

tables.description: Mean proportion correct scores with respect to task, age group, and sound condition. Error bars denote the bootstrapped confidence intervals.
Mean proportion correct scores in the verbal task in two consecutive blocks of four trials each. Error bars denote the bootstrapped confidence intervals.

limitations: The study did not include nonspeech sounds, which would be necessary to fully differentiate between phonological and non-phonological interference.
The study did not include phonological processing tasks that do not require serial order retention, limiting the ability to specify the exact mechanism of interference.
The current findings do not allow a clear specification of the mechanism that evokes the proposed interference with phonological codes.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items in children and adults
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractImmediate serial recall of visually presented items is reliably impaired by task-irrelevant speech that the participants are instructed to ignore (“irrelevant speech effect,” ISE). The ISE is stronger with changing speech tokens (words or syllables) when compared to repetitions of single tokens (“changing-state effect,” CSE). These phenomena have been attributed to sound-induced diversions of attention away from the focal task (attention capture account), or to specific interference of obligatory, involuntary sound processing with either the integrity of phonological traces in a phonological short-term store (phonological loop account), or the efficiency of a domain-general rehearsal process employed for serial order retention (changing-state account). Aiming to further explore the role of attention, phonological coding, and serial order retention in the ISE, we analyzed the effects of steady-state and changing-state speech on serial order reconstruction of visually presented verbal and spatial items in children (n = 81) and adults (n = 80). In the verbal task, both age groups performed worse with changing-state speech (sequences of different syllables) when compared with steady-state speech (one syllable repeated) and silence. Children were more impaired than adults by both speech sounds. In the spatial task, no disruptive effect of irrelevant speech was found in either group. These results indicate that irrelevant speech evokes similarity-based interference, and thus pose difficulties for the attention-capture and the changing-state account of the ISE.
